title: What is the Raft consensus algorithm — a protocol for achieving agreement across a cluster of nodes on a shared log, using leader election (candidates request votes, majority wins), log replication (the leader appends entries and replicates to followers, committing when a majority acknowledges), and safety (committed entries are never lost even if the leader changes) — and where is it used in practice (etcd for Kubernetes, Consul for service discovery, Kafka KRaft replacing ZooKeeper for metadata consensus)?
shortTitle: What is the Raft consensus algorithm, and where is it used in practice?

s1_definition.profdef: Raft is a consensus algorithm that lets a cluster of nodes agree on a single, consistent, ordered log of commands even when nodes fail or messages are delayed. It works through three mechanisms. Leader election: time is divided into terms, and in each term nodes elect a single leader; a candidate requests votes and becomes leader if it wins a majority. Log replication: all client commands go to the leader, which appends them to its log and replicates them to followers, and an entry is committed once a majority of nodes have stored it. Safety: Raft's voting and commit rules guarantee that a committed entry is never lost and never contradicted, even across leader changes, so every node applies the same commands in the same order. Because commitment requires a majority (a quorum), Raft tolerates the failure of a minority of nodes while remaining correct, which is why it underpins the control planes of etcd (Kubernetes), Consul (service discovery), and Kafka's KRaft metadata layer.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India has five branch managers who must all keep an identical master ledger, and no single entry is official until most of them have written it down, so that even if a couple of managers are unreachable, the bank still agrees on what happened. Raft is the rulebook for this. First the managers elect one head manager for the day; whoever gets votes from the majority wins. Then every new ledger entry goes only to the head manager, who writes it and sends copies to the others; the entry becomes official only once more than half the managers have recorded it. And the rules are designed so that once an entry is official, it can never be erased or changed, even if tomorrow a different manager takes over as head. So long as a majority of managers are present, the bank always has one agreed, unchangeable ledger.
s1_definition.oneliner: Raft makes a cluster agree on one ordered log via an elected leader, majority-quorum commits, and safety rules that preserve committed entries across leader changes — and it is the backbone of etcd, Consul, and Kafka KRaft.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Raft is a consensus algorithm that lets a cluster of nodes agree on a single, consistent, ordered log of commands even when nodes fail or messages are delayed. It works through three mechanisms. Leader election: time is divided into terms, and in each term nodes elect a single leader; a candidate requests votes and becomes leader if it wins a majority. Log replication: all client commands go to the leader, which appends them to its log and replicates them to followers, and an entry is committed once a majority of nodes have stored it. Safety: Raft's voting and commit rules guarantee that a committed entry is never lost and never contradicted, even across leader changes, so every node applies the same commands in the same order. Because commitment requires a majority (a quorum), Raft tolerates the failure of a minority of nodes while remaining correct, which is why it underpins the control planes of etcd (Kubernetes), Consul (service discovery), and Kafka's KRaft metadata layer.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India has five branch managers who must all keep an identical master ledger, and no single entry is official until most of them have written it down, so that even if a couple of managers are unreachable, the bank still agrees on what happened. Raft is the rulebook for this. First the managers elect one head manager for the day; whoever gets votes from the majority wins. Then every new ledger entry goes only to the head manager, who writes it and sends copies to the others; the entry becomes official only once more than half the managers have recorded it. And the rules are designed so that once an entry is official, it can never be erased or changed, even if tomorrow a different manager takes over as head. So long as a majority of managers are present, the bank always has one agreed, unchangeable ledger.

**One line to remember:** Raft makes a cluster agree on one ordered log via an elected leader, majority-quorum commits, and safety rules that preserve committed entries across leader changes — and it is the backbone of etcd, Consul, and Kafka KRaft.

sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India, a cluster of configuration nodes must agree on a single source of truth for critical settings — for example which data centre is currently the primary for transfers — and this agreement must survive node failures without ever producing two conflicting answers.

Problem 1 — if each node independently decides the primary, a network glitch could leave two nodes both believing they are primary, and transfers could be double-processed. The bank needs exactly one agreed decision at a time.

Problem 2 — the decision must remain correct even if a node crashes, so it cannot depend on any single node; it needs a majority-based agreement that tolerates a minority failing.

The mini-project simulates a small Raft cluster: nodes hold terms and logs, run a leader election requiring a majority of votes, replicate a configuration-change entry from the leader, and commit it only when a majority acknowledge. The demo elects a leader, replicates a "primary = DC1" entry committed by majority, then fails the leader and shows a new leader elected by the remaining majority with the committed entry preserved, demonstrating leader election, majority-commit replication, and safety across a leader change.
sections.s5_journey:
Input: a five-node Raft cluster must agree on which data centre is primary, survive the leader crashing, and never lose a committed decision.

Step 1 — Leader election. One node becomes a candidate, increments its term, votes for itself, and requests votes from the others. Each peer grants its vote because the candidate's log is at least as up to date. The candidate collects three votes, which is the majority of five, so it becomes the leader for that term. The cluster now has exactly one leader.

Step 2 — Replicate a configuration entry. A client asks to set the primary to DC1. The leader appends the entry PRIMARY equals DC1 to its own log and sends it to the followers. Five nodes store it, which is well past the majority of three, so the leader marks the entry committed and the followers do too. The decision is now official and identical on every node.

Step 3 — Confirm the commit. The cluster reports that a surviving node holds the committed entry PRIMARY equals DC1 at its log index. This is the single agreed source of truth.

Step 4 — Leader crashes. The leader node fails and stops responding. Because the entry PRIMARY equals DC1 was already committed on a majority, it exists on the surviving four nodes, so the crash cannot erase it. This is the safety guarantee.

Step 5 — Re-election preserves safety. The remaining four nodes, still a majority, elect a new leader. The safety rules ensure the new leader has the committed entry, so after the leader change the committed PRIMARY equals DC1 is still present. The new leader then continues the log by replicating a further entry. Throughout a leader failure, the committed decision was never lost and the cluster never produced two conflicting answers.

```
2026-10-24 19:46:28 [INFO] ELECTED leader node-1 term 1 with 5 votes (quorum 3)
2026-10-24 19:46:28 [INFO] COMMITTED 'PRIMARY=DC1' at index 1 (5/5 stored, quorum 3)
2026-10-24 19:46:28 [INFO] After commit: node node-1 has committed 'PRIMARY=DC1' (index 1)
2026-10-24 19:46:28 [WARNING] Leader node-1 CRASHES
2026-10-24 19:46:28 [INFO] ELECTED leader node-2 term 2 with 4 votes (quorum 3)
2026-10-24 19:46:28 [INFO] After leader change: node node-2 has committed 'PRIMARY=DC1' (index 1)
2026-10-24 19:46:28 [INFO] COMMITTED 'PRIMARY=DC2' at index 2 (4/4 stored, quorum 3)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  5-node Raft cluster (quorum = 3)
    │
    ▼ ELECTION: candidate requests votes → majority (3+) → LEADER (term 1)
    │
    ▼ REPLICATION: client cmd PRIMARY=DC1 → leader appends → AppendEntries to followers
    │   majority store (5/5 ≥ 3) → COMMITTED → applied on all
    │
    ▼ SAFETY: committed entry lives on the majority
    │
    ├─ LEADER CRASHES (node-1 down) → PRIMARY=DC1 still on surviving 4
    ▼
  RE-ELECTION: surviving majority (4) elects new leader (term 2)
    new leader HAS committed PRIMARY=DC1 (safety) → continues log → PRIMARY=DC2
  No conflicting decision ever; committed entry never lost.
```

```
  ═══ LLD — Raft Mechanics ═══

  ┌─ Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ Replicated State Machine: same log → same state everywhere │
  │ Quorum (majority) commit: tolerate minority failures       │
  │ Strong-leader: all writes through one leader per term      │
  │ Randomised election timeout: avoid split votes             │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID ───────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ S: Node holds state; Cluster runs election + replication   │
  │ O: new command type = new log entry, protocol unchanged    │
  │ D: Cluster depends on RaftNode abstraction                 │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ──
  ┌──────────────┐ manages ┌──────────────┐ holds ┌──────────────┐
  │ RaftCluster  │────────▶│ RaftNode     │──────▶│ LogEntry     │
  │ + electLeader│         │ term, state  │       │ term,index,  │
  │ + replicate  │         │ votedFor     │       │ command,     │
  │ + quorum()   │         │ log[]        │       │ committed    │
  └──────────────┘         └──────────────┘       └──────────────┘

  ── State Diagram: a node's role ──
  [FOLLOWER] ──election timeout──→ [CANDIDATE] ──majority votes──→ [LEADER]
       ▲                                │ loses / higher term seen        │
       └────────────────────────────────┴────── steps down ──────────────┘

  ── Call Chain (main) ──
  1. cluster.electLeader()           → majority votes → node-1 LEADER
  2. cluster.replicate(leader, DC1)  → majority store → COMMITTED
  3. leader.alive = false             → crash
  4. cluster.electLeader()           → surviving majority → node-2 LEADER
  5. reportCommitted()                → PRIMARY=DC1 preserved (safety)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Raft is a consensus algorithm that lets a cluster of nodes agree on a single, consistent, ordered log of commands even when some nodes crash or messages are delayed, and it was deliberately designed to be understandable by splitting the problem into three parts: leader election, log replication, and safety. For leader election, Raft divides time into numbered terms, and in each term the nodes elect one leader: a node that stops hearing heartbeats becomes a candidate, increments the term, votes for itself, and requests votes from the others, becoming leader only if it wins a majority. Randomised election timeouts make split votes rare, so the cluster reliably settles on exactly one leader per term.

For log replication, all client commands flow through the leader, which appends each command to its own log and replicates it to the followers with AppendEntries messages, and an entry becomes committed only once a majority of nodes have stored it. Because every node applies committed entries in the same order, all the state machines stay identical. For safety, Raft's rules guarantee that a committed entry is never lost or contradicted even when leaders change: a node only grants its vote to a candidate whose log is at least as up to date, so a node missing committed entries can never win an election; a new leader never deletes committed entries, only brings followers into line; and these rules together ensure every future leader already has every committed entry. The whole thing rests on a quorum: commitment needs a strict majority, so a five-node cluster tolerates two failures and a three-node cluster tolerates one, which is why Raft clusters are sized at odd numbers.

In practice Raft powers the coordination and metadata planes of major systems. etcd uses Raft to store Kubernetes cluster state so every control-plane component reads the same truth. Consul uses Raft to keep its service catalog and key-value store consistent for service discovery and configuration. Kafka's KRaft mode uses a Raft-based metadata log to replace ZooKeeper, so brokers agree on topic, partition, and leadership metadata without a separate coordination system. The nuance I would stress is that Raft is used for the small, critical, strongly-consistent state — who is the leader, what is the configuration, cluster membership — not for the bulk, high-throughput data plane, because requiring a majority to acknowledge every write would not scale to millions of transactions.

In my banking work this distinction mattered: I would use a Raft-backed store like etcd to agree on something small and critical, such as which data centre is the current primary for transfers or a distributed lock ensuring only one node runs a settlement job, while the actual transaction throughput is handled by the data store that Raft coordinates. The demo I think about is a five-node cluster that elects a leader by majority, commits a primary-selection entry once a majority store it, then loses the leader and re-elects a new one that still has the committed decision — proving that a committed entry survives a leader change and the cluster never produces two conflicting answers. The principle I take into interviews is that Raft gives you a strongly-consistent, fault-tolerant agreed log for the small critical state that must never diverge, and knowing that it belongs in the coordination plane rather than the data plane is what separates genuinely understanding it from merely naming it.
